Cathy was a powerful ally at home; and between them they at length persuaded my
master to acquiesce in their having a ride or a walk together about once a
week, under my guardianship, and on the moors nearest the Grange: for June
found him still declining. Though he had set aside yearly a portion of his
income for my young lady’s fortune, he had a natural desire that she
might retain—or at least return in a short time to—the house of her
ancestors; and he considered her only prospect of doing that was by a union
with his heir; he had no idea that the latter was failing almost as fast as
himself; nor had any one, I believe: no doctor visited the Heights, and no one
saw Master Heathcliff to make report of his condition among us. I, for my part,
began to fancy my forebodings were false, and that he must be actually
rallying, when he mentioned riding and walking on the moors, and seemed so
earnest in pursuing his object. I could not picture a father treating a dying
child as tyrannically and wickedly as I afterwards learned Heathcliff had
treated him, to compel this apparent eagerness: his efforts redoubling the more
imminently his avaricious and unfeeling plans were threatened with defeat by
death.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Describes the final persuasion of Edgar to permit the meetings, his declining health, and Nelly's devastating blindness to Heathcliff's tyranny of the equally dying Linton—a tragic miscalculation with vast consequences.
enrichment.best_quote: I could not picture a father treating a dying child as tyrannically and wickedly as I afterwards learned Heathcliff had treated him, to compel this apparent eagerness: his efforts redoubling the more imminently his avaricious and unfeeling plans were threatened with defeat by death.
enrichment.summary: Cathy and Edgar together persuade the failing Edgar to permit weekly rides or walks with Linton on the moors, which Edgar accepts because he hopes Linton might inherit and restore Cathy to Thrushcross Grange; Nelly naively interprets Linton's eagerness for outings as a sign of recovery, unaware of Heathcliff's cruel coercion.

context: This passage concludes a section where Mrs. Dean recounts how Edgar Linton, weakening from illness, reluctantly permits his daughter Catherine to meet with his sickly cousin Linton Heathcliff on the moors under supervision. Edgar hopes their union will preserve Catherine's inheritance of Thrushcross Grange, unaware that Linton is dying and that Heathcliff is manipulating his son to secure the property through marriage to Catherine.

text:
Summer was already past its prime, when Edgar reluctantly yielded his assent to
their entreaties, and Catherine and I set out on our first ride to join her
cousin. It was a close, sultry day: devoid of sunshine, but with a sky too
dappled and hazy to threaten rain: and our place of meeting had been fixed at
the guide-stone, by the cross-roads. On arriving there, however, a little
herd-boy, despatched as a messenger, told us that,—“Maister Linton
wer just o’ this side th’ Heights: and he’d be mitch obleeged
to us to gang on a bit further.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Opening scene-setting with plot mechanics; establishes the first meeting between Cathy and Linton but lacks dramatic tension at this stage.
enrichment.summary: Edgar agrees to let Cathy visit her cousin Linton. They meet at the guide-stone, but a messenger tells them Linton has moved further toward the Heights.

context: This is the opening of the chapter where Nelly Dean and Catherine embark on their first visit to see Linton Heathcliff at his request. Edgar has reluctantly permitted the outing, and they travel to meet him at the guide-stone, only to be directed further toward Wuthering Heights by a messenger boy.

text:
“Then Master Linton has forgot the first injunction of his uncle,”
I observed: “he bid us keep on the Grange land, and here we are off at
once.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nelly observes Linton's breach of Edgar's instructions; hints at tension between the Heights and the Grange estates.
enrichment.best_quote: he bid us keep on the Grange land, and here we are off at once.
enrichment.summary: Nelly notes that Linton has already violated Edgar's instruction to remain on Grange land.

context: The narrator and Catherine have arrived at the meeting point to visit Linton Heathcliff, but a messenger tells them Linton is waiting further away, off the Grange land. The narrator comments that Linton has violated his uncle Edgar's instruction to stay on Grange property.

text:
“Well, we’ll turn our horses’ heads round when we reach
him,” answered my companion; “our excursion shall lie towards
home.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's practical reassurance about returning home; purely transitional dialogue without substance.
enrichment.summary: Cathy suggests they will turn back toward the Grange once they meet Linton.

context: Catherine's companion (the narrator) agrees to turn back toward home once they reach Linton, after the narrator has pointed out that Master Linton has violated his uncle Edgar's instruction to keep to the Grange land by asking them to meet him closer to Wuthering Heights.

text:
But when we reached him, and that was scarcely a quarter of a mile from his own
door, we found he had no horse; and we were forced to dismount, and leave ours
to graze. He lay on the heath, awaiting our approach, and did not rise till we
came within a few yards. Then he walked so feebly, and looked so pale, that I
immediately exclaimed,—“Why, Master Heathcliff, you are not fit for
enjoying a ramble this morning. How ill you do look!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's physical deterioration is immediately apparent and alarming; foreshadows his manipulation and vulnerability.
enrichment.best_quote: he walked so feebly, and looked so pale
enrichment.summary: Linton appears frail and pale, unable to ride; Nelly remarks on his obvious illness.

context: Catherine and the narrator ride out to meet Linton Heathcliff at the guide-stone, but find him waiting on the heath near his home instead. Upon arrival, they discover he has no horse and must dismount. The narrator is immediately struck by Linton's frail appearance and poor health, expressing concern about his fitness for the outing.

text:
Catherine surveyed him with grief and astonishment: she changed the ejaculation
of joy on her lips to one of alarm; and the congratulation on their
long-postponed meeting to an anxious inquiry, whether he were worse than usual?

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's reaction shows her emotional investment but is largely expected; demonstrates her capacity for sympathy.
enrichment.summary: Cathy's joy at seeing Linton turns to alarm upon witnessing his poor health.

context: Catherine and the narrator arrive to meet Linton Heathcliff for their planned outing. Upon seeing him lying weakly on the heath, Catherine's initial joy at their reunion turns to concern as she observes his poor physical condition and asks if he is worse than usual.

text:
“No—better—better!” he panted, trembling, and retaining
her hand as if he needed its support, while his large blue eyes wandered
timidly over her; the hollowness round them transforming to haggard wildness
the languid expression they once possessed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's physical and emotional fragility are powerfully rendered; his dependent clinging and haunted gaze suggest paternal control.
enrichment.best_quote: the hollowness round them transforming to haggard wildness the languid expression they once possessed
enrichment.summary: Linton insists he is better but trembles and clings to Cathy's hand; his eyes betray inner distress.

context: Linton Heathcliff, appearing pale and weak, greets Catherine and the narrator on the heath. When Catherine expresses concern about his poor health, he insists he is better while trembling and clinging to her hand, his eyes revealing the physical toll of his illness despite his denial.

text:
“But you have been worse,” persisted his cousin; “worse than
when I saw you last; you are thinner, and—”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy observes Linton's deterioration; routine acknowledgment of his worsened condition.
enrichment.summary: Cathy notes that Linton has worsened since they last met and is thinner.

context: Catherine observes that Linton appears physically deteriorated since their last meeting, noting he has become thinner and weaker, despite his claims of improvement.

text:
“I’m tired,” he interrupted, hurriedly. “It is too hot
for walking, let us rest here. And, in the morning, I often feel
sick—papa says I grow so fast.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's defensive evasion and his attribution of illness to growth are suspicious; hints at hidden suffering.
enrichment.best_quote: papa says I grow so fast
enrichment.summary: Linton dismisses his illness, blaming heat and rapid growth, and proposes rest.

context: Linton Heathcliff, appearing pale and weak during Catherine's visit to the moors, makes excuses for his poor health, claiming fatigue and rapid growth rather than admitting to serious illness, while Catherine and the narrator grow concerned about his deteriorating condition.

text: Badly satisfied, Cathy sat down, and he reclined beside her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief narrative transition with minimal content; Cathy and Linton settle.
enrichment.summary: Cathy sits; Linton reclines beside her.

context: Catherine and the narrator meet Linton Heathcliff on the moors for a planned visit. Upon arrival, they find him pale and weak, lying on the heath. When Catherine expresses concern about his poor health, Linton insists he is better and suggests they rest together on the spot rather than continue walking in the heat.

text:
“This is something like your paradise,” said she, making an effort
at cheerfulness. “You recollect the two days we agreed to spend in the
place and way each thought pleasantest? This is nearly yours, only there are
clouds; but then they are so soft and mellow: it is nicer than sunshine. Next
week, if you can, we’ll ride down to the Grange Park, and try
mine.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's attempted cheerfulness and reference to their imagined shared paradise hints at her romantic feeling for Linton.
enrichment.best_quote: This is something like your paradise
enrichment.summary: Cathy attempts to engage Linton by recalling their earlier conversation about ideal places to spend time together.

context: Catherine attempts to lift Linton's spirits during their meeting on the heath by reminding him of a shared plan they had made to spend time in their ideal locations. She tries to engage him cheerfully by suggesting his preferred spot resembles paradise, and proposes visiting her own favorite place the following week, hoping to revive his interest and improve his melancholy mood.

text:
Linton did not appear to remember what she talked of; and he had evidently
great difficulty in sustaining any kind of conversation. His lack of interest
in the subjects she started, and his equal incapacity to contribute to her
entertainment, were so obvious that she could not conceal her disappointment.
An indefinite alteration had come over his whole person and manner. The
pettishness that might be caressed into fondness, had yielded to a listless
apathy; there was less of the peevish temper of a child which frets and teases
on purpose to be soothed, and more of the self-absorbed moroseness of a
confirmed invalid, repelling consolation, and ready to regard the good-humoured
mirth of others as an insult. Catherine perceived, as well as I did, that he
held it rather a punishment, than a gratification, to endure our company; and
she made no scruple of proposing, presently, to depart. That proposal,
unexpectedly, roused Linton from his lethargy, and threw him into a strange
state of agitation. He glanced fearfully towards the Heights, begging she would
remain another half-hour, at least.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Penetrating analysis of Linton's psychological transformation; his shift from peevish child to listless invalid reveals the cost of Heathcliff's control and foreshadows the danger of this match.
enrichment.best_quote: The pettishness that might be caressed into fondness, had yielded to a listless apathy; there was less of the peevish temper of a child which frets and teases on purpose to be soothed, and more of the self-absorbed moroseness of a confirmed invalid, repelling consolation, and ready to regard the good-humoured mirth of others as an insult.
enrichment.summary: Nelly observes Linton's complete change in character: from a child seeking attention to a withdrawn invalid who sees others' company as a burden. Cathy perceives his discomfort and proposes leaving.

context: Catherine and the narrator visit Linton at the guide-stone to spend time together as planned. Upon arrival, they find Linton pale and weak, lying on the heath without a horse. Catherine is disappointed to discover that Linton has become withdrawn and apathetic, showing little interest in conversation or her company. When she proposes to leave, Linton becomes agitated and fearfully begs her to stay longer, glancing anxiously toward Wuthering Heights.

text:
“But I think,” said Cathy, “you’d be more comfortable
at home than sitting here; and I cannot amuse you to-day, I see, by my tales,
and songs, and chatter: you have grown wiser than I, in these six months; you
have little taste for my diversions now: or else, if I could amuse you,
I’d willingly stay.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's polite but frustrated attempt to leave; demonstrates her disappointment in Linton but also her compassion.
enrichment.best_quote: you have grown wiser than I, in these six months; you have little taste for my diversions now
enrichment.summary: Cathy suggests leaving since she cannot amuse Linton, noting his seeming maturation away from childish pleasures.

context: Catherine suggests to the ailing Linton that he would be more comfortable at home, acknowledging his apparent lack of interest in her company and entertainment during their first meeting since summer began.

text:
“Stay to rest yourself,” he replied. “And, Catherine,
don’t think or say that I’m  very  unwell: it is the heavy
weather and heat that make me dull; and I walked about, before you came, a
great deal for me. Tell uncle I’m in tolerable health, will you?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's desperate plea to stay and his manipulation of Cathy; reveals his fear of Heathcliff and sets up the trap.
enrichment.best_quote: Tell uncle I'm in tolerable health, will you?
enrichment.summary: Linton asks Cathy to stay and lie to her father about his health, hinting at his distress and manipulation.

context: Linton asks Catherine to reassure her father (his uncle) that he is in good health, attributing his listlessness to the weather rather than illness, while secretly asking her not to reveal his true poor condition to his father Heathcliff.

text:
“I’ll tell him that  you  say so, Linton. I couldn’t
affirm that you are,” observed my young lady, wondering at his
pertinacious assertion of what was evidently an untruth.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's honest assessment contrasts with Linton's false claim; shows her perception but also her hesitation to confront the lie.
enrichment.best_quote: I'll tell him that you say so, Linton. I couldn't affirm that you are
enrichment.summary: Cathy gently refuses to confirm Linton's claim of good health, seeing through his falsehood.

context: Catherine and the narrator visit Linton Heathcliff on the moors. Linton appears gravely ill and weak, though he insists he is in "tolerable health." Catherine expresses skepticism about his claims, noting his obvious physical deterioration and refusing to lie to her father about Linton's true condition.

text:
“And be here again next Thursday,” continued he, shunning her
puzzled gaze. “And give him my thanks for permitting you to come—my
best thanks, Catherine. And—and, if you  did  meet my father, and he
asked you about me, don’t lead him to suppose that I’ve been
extremely silent and stupid: don’t look sad and downcast, as you
 are  doing—he’ll be angry.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's urgent plea for Cathy to return and his fear of his father's reaction reveals the coercive trap; this is the emotional crux of his manipulation.
enrichment.best_quote: And be here again next Thursday... Don't provoke him against me, Catherine, for he is very hard
enrichment.summary: Linton urgently asks Cathy to return weekly and implores her not to reveal his poor state to Heathcliff, fearing his father's wrath.

context: Linton anxiously asks Catherine to return the following Thursday and instructs her to conceal his poor health and withdrawn behavior from his father Heathcliff, fearing his father's anger if he learns the truth about Linton's condition.

text:
“I care nothing for his anger,” exclaimed Cathy, imagining she
would be its object.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's declaration of fearlessness toward Heathcliff; routine bravado that misreads the danger.
enrichment.best_quote: I care nothing for his anger
enrichment.summary: Cathy asserts that Heathcliff's anger does not concern her.

context: Catherine and Linton meet for a ride, but she finds him physically weak and emotionally distant. When Linton anxiously begs her not to provoke his father Heathcliff against him, Catherine dismissively declares she cares nothing for Heathcliff's anger, assuming the threat is directed at herself rather than understanding Linton's fear of his father's cruelty toward him.

text:
“But I do,” said her cousin, shuddering. “ Don’t 
provoke him against me, Catherine, for he is very hard.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's fear of Heathcliff is acute and visceral; his use of 'shuddering' and direct appeal underscores his terror and Heathcliff's power.
enrichment.best_quote: But I do... Don't provoke him against me, Catherine, for he is very hard
enrichment.summary: Linton shudders and urgently warns Cathy not to anger his father, revealing his deep fear.

context: Linton begs Catherine not to provoke his father Heathcliff against him, revealing his fear of paternal cruelty and his anxiety about how his father perceives him during Catherine's visit to the Heights.

text:
“Is he severe to you, Master Heathcliff?” I inquired. “Has he
grown weary of indulgence, and passed from passive to active hatred?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nelly's probing question suggests awareness of Heathcliff's capacity for cruelty and his change from passive to active hatred.
enrichment.best_quote: Has he grown weary of indulgence, and passed from passive to active hatred?
enrichment.summary: Nelly questions whether Heathcliff has become actively cruel to Linton after years of indifference.

context: The narrator questions Linton about his father Heathcliff's treatment of him, suspecting that Heathcliff may have shifted from neglect to active cruelty. This occurs during Catherine and the narrator's visit to Linton on the moors, after they notice his severe physical decline and fearful demeanor, particularly his anxiety about his father's potential arrival.

text:
Linton looked at me, but did not answer; and, after keeping her seat by his
side another ten minutes, during which his head fell drowsily on his breast,
and he uttered nothing except suppressed moans of exhaustion or pain, Cathy
began to seek solace in looking for bilberries, and sharing the produce of her
researches with me: she did not offer them to him, for she saw further notice
would only weary and annoy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's exhaustion and Cathy's compassionate distraction show the deepening pity that makes her vulnerable to further manipulation.
enrichment.best_quote: his head fell drowsily on his breast, and he uttered nothing except suppressed moans of exhaustion or pain
enrichment.summary: Linton falls into an exhausted sleep while Cathy gathers bilberries to keep herself occupied.

context: This passage occurs during Catherine and the narrator's first visit to meet Linton on the heath. After Linton has anxiously asked the narrator not to provoke his father Heathcliff against him, he falls into an exhausted sleep. While waiting for him to wake, Catherine occupies herself gathering bilberries, having realized that further attempts to engage the sickly and withdrawn Linton would only distress him.

text:
“Is it half-an-hour now, Ellen?” she whispered in my ear, at last.
“I can’t tell why we should stay. He’s asleep, and papa will
be wanting us back.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's practical impatience; routine observation about time and duty.
enrichment.summary: Cathy whispers to Nelly, asking if half an hour has passed and wondering about returning home.

context: Catherine grows impatient during her visit with the sickly Linton Heathcliff on the moors. She whispers to Ellen (the narrator) asking if half an hour has passed, expressing her desire to leave since Linton has fallen asleep and her father will be expecting their return.

text:
“Well, we must not leave him asleep,” I answered; “wait till
he wakes, and be patient. You were mighty eager to set off, but your longing to
see poor Linton has soon evaporated!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nelly's mild rebuke about patience; routine narrative device emphasizing Cathy's waning interest.
enrichment.summary: Nelly insists they wait for Linton to wake, gently teasing Cathy about her fading eagerness.

context: Ellen (the narrator) urges Catherine to wait for Linton to wake before they leave their meeting place, noting Catherine's initial eagerness to see her cousin has diminished now that she finds him listless and unwell.

text:
“Why did  he  wish to see me?” returned Catherine. “In
his crossest humours, formerly, I liked him better than I do in his present
curious mood. It’s just as if it were a task he was compelled to
perform—this interview—for fear his father should scold him. But
I’m hardly going to come to give Mr. Heathcliff pleasure; whatever reason
he may have for ordering Linton to undergo this penance. And, though I’m
glad he’s better in health, I’m sorry he’s so much less
pleasant, and so much less affectionate to me.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's acute perception of Linton's reluctance and her realization that the visit is coerced; demonstrates her growing skepticism but also her susceptibility to Heathcliff's trap.
enrichment.best_quote: It's just as if it were a task he was compelled to perform—this interview—for fear his father should scold him
enrichment.summary: Cathy astutely observes that Linton treats the visit as an unwelcome obligation imposed by his father, resenting being used as a pawn.

context: Catherine expresses her disappointment and suspicion about Linton's behavior during their meeting. She questions whether Linton genuinely wanted to see her or is merely obeying his father Heathcliff's orders, noting his withdrawn demeanor and lack of affection compared to before. She contrasts his previous peevishness, which she could tolerate, with his current apathetic and morose state, suggesting he views their time together as an unwelcome obligation rather than a pleasure.

text: “You think  he is  better in health, then?” I said.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nelly's brief probing question about Cathy's assessment of Linton's health; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Nelly asks whether Cathy truly believes Linton is in better health.

context: The narrator questions Catherine's assessment of Linton's health after observing his pale, weakened appearance during their meeting on the moors. Catherine has just suggested Linton is better because he exaggerates his suffering, but the narrator suspects the opposite—that Linton is actually worse.

text:
“Yes,” she answered; “because he always made such a great
deal of his sufferings, you know. He is not tolerably well, as he told me to
tell papa; but he’s better, very likely.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's rationalization of Linton's claims; shows her desire to believe him despite contrary evidence.
enrichment.summary: Cathy rationalizes that Linton likely exaggerates his sufferings and is probably truly improving.

context: Catherine defends her assessment that Linton is in better health, attributing his complaints to his tendency to exaggerate his suffering, while acknowledging his own claim of being "tolerably well."

text:
“There you differ with me, Miss Cathy,” I remarked; “I should
conjecture him to be far worse.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Nelly's direct contradiction of Cathy's judgment; establishes the trustworthy observer's assessment against Cathy's wishful thinking.
enrichment.best_quote: I should conjecture him to be far worse
enrichment.summary: Nelly flatly asserts her conviction that Linton is in worse health than Cathy believes.

context: The narrator disagrees with Catherine's assessment of Linton's health during their visit to the moors. While Catherine believes Linton is better because he downplays his suffering, the narrator observes that Linton actually appears far worse—pale, weak, and showing signs of serious illness. This exchange highlights the narrator's concern about Linton's deteriorating condition and foreshadows the troubling circumstances surrounding him.

text:
Linton here started from his slumber in bewildered terror, and asked if any one
had called his name.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's sudden terror at waking and his hallucinatory fear of his father; reinforces his psychological torment.
enrichment.summary: Linton wakes in terror, convinced someone called his name, apparently fearful of his father.

context: Catherine and the narrator have been visiting the sickly Linton Heathcliff on the moors. While Linton sleeps, Catherine and the narrator discuss his deteriorating health and changed demeanor. Linton suddenly awakens in fear, thinking he heard his father calling him.

text:
“No,” said Catherine; “unless in dreams. I cannot conceive
how you manage to doze out of doors, in the morning.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's calm reassurance; routine response that masks the darker implications of Linton's fear.
enrichment.summary: Cathy assures Linton that no one called him; she suggests he was dreaming.

context: Catherine and the narrator visit Linton Heathcliff on the moors. During their meeting, Linton appears ill and weak, falling asleep while they wait. Catherine wakes him, and he anxiously asks if anyone called his name, fearing his father's approach. Catherine reassures him that only she and Ellen were discussing his health.

text:
“I thought I heard my father,” he gasped, glancing up to the
frowning nab above us. “You are sure nobody spoke?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's continued panic and his glance toward the Heights; viscerally conveys his living dread of Heathcliff.
enrichment.best_quote: I thought I heard my father
enrichment.summary: Linton gasps and looks toward the frowning hills above, still convinced his father is near.

context: Linton, appearing ill and anxious during a visit from Catherine and the narrator, suddenly wakes from sleep in terror, fearing his father Heathcliff is approaching. He asks if anyone called his name, revealing his deep fear of his father's presence and anger.

text:
“Quite sure,” replied his cousin. “Only Ellen and I were
disputing concerning your health. Are you truly stronger, Linton, than when we
separated in winter? If you be, I’m certain one thing is not
stronger—your regard for me: speak,—are you?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's direct test of Linton's affection, couched in casual conversation; her demand for reassurance shows emotional investment despite her growing disillusionment.

context: Catherine and Linton have met on the heath for their first visit in months. Linton appears gravely ill and weak, causing Catherine concern. After he falls asleep, Catherine and Ellen discuss whether his health has actually improved. When Linton suddenly wakes in terror, thinking he heard his father's voice, Catherine seizes the moment to directly question him about his physical condition and, more pointedly, about the apparent decline in his affection toward her.

text:

am!” And, still under the spell of the imaginary voice, his gaze wandered

text:
Cathy rose. “For to-day we must part,” she said. “And I
won’t conceal that I have been sadly disappointed with our meeting;
though I’ll mention it to nobody but you: not that I stand in awe of Mr.
Heathcliff.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cathy's decision to depart and her confession of disappointment; demonstrates her growing awareness of the situation's artificiality while maintaining her claim of independence.

context: Catherine prepares to leave after a disappointing visit with her sickly cousin Linton. She confides in the narrator (Ellen) that she is disappointed by Linton's withdrawn behavior and lack of affection, though she assures Ellen she will not reveal this disappointment to others or show fear of Linton's father, Heathcliff.

text:
“Hush,” murmured Linton; “for God’s sake, hush!
He’s coming.” And he clung to Catherine’s arm, striving to
detain her; but at that announcement she hastily disengaged herself, and
whistled to Minny, who obeyed her like a dog.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's desperate clinging and his fear of Heathcliff's imminent arrival set the trap; Cathy's swift, decisive departure and whistle to her horse show her instinctive good judgment.

During their meeting, Linton appears gravely ill and anxious, repeatedly glancing toward Wuthering Heights and expressing fear of his father Heathcliff. As Catherine prepares to leave, disappointed by Linton's withdrawn behavior, Linton suddenly claims his father is approaching and desperately tries to keep her from departing, but Catherine quickly mounts her horse and rides away.

text:
“I’ll be here next Thursday,” she cried, springing to the
saddle. “Good-bye. Quick, Ellen!”

enrichment.best_quote: I'll be here next Thursday

text:
And so we left him, scarcely conscious of our departure, so absorbed was he in
anticipating his father’s approach.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Linton's absorption in anticipating Heathcliff's arrival; reinforces his psychological slavery and the danger lurking.

context: Catherine and the narrator visit Linton Heathcliff on the moors. They find him physically weak and emotionally distant. When Linton becomes terrified at the thought of his father Heathcliff approaching, Catherine decides to leave. Linton clings to her in fear, but she hastily departs on horseback, leaving him anxious and preoccupied with his father's imminent arrival.

text:
Before we reached home, Catherine’s displeasure softened into a perplexed
sensation of pity and regret, largely blended with vague, uneasy doubts about
Linton’s actual circumstances, physical and social: in which I partook,
though I counselled her not to say much; for a second journey would make us
better judges. My master requested an account of our ongoings. His
nephew’s offering of thanks was duly delivered, Miss Cathy gently
touching on the rest: I also threw little light on his inquiries, for I hardly
knew what to hide and what to reveal.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reflection on the visit's implications; Nelly and Cathy's shared concern and the deliberate reticence about revealing the truth signal their growing awareness of a dark scheme.
enrichment.summary: On the return journey, Cathy's disappointment transforms into pity and uneasy doubt about Linton's welfare. When Edgar asks about the visit, they conceal the truth, uncertain what to reveal, suggesting tacit recognition of darker forces at work.

context: This passage concludes the chapter, occurring after Catherine and the narrator depart from their meeting with the sickly Linton Heathcliff on the moors. Catherine's initial disappointment with Linton's withdrawn and listless behavior transforms into concern and confusion about his true condition and circumstances. Upon returning home, the narrator and Catherine report to Edgar Linton (Catherine's father) about the visit, carefully withholding details while delivering Linton's thanks, both uncertain about what information should be disclosed regarding Heathcliff's treatment of his son.

A charming introduction to a hermit’s life! Four weeks’ torture,
tossing, and sickness! Oh, these bleak winds and bitter northern skies, and
impassable roads, and dilatory country surgeons! And oh, this dearth of the
human physiognomy! and, worse than all, the terrible intimation of Kenneth that
I need not expect to be out of doors till spring!

enrichment.interest_rationale: A comic complaint by Lockwood about his illness and isolation, establishing his unreliable character voice.
enrichment.best_quote: Four weeks' torture, tossing, and sickness!
enrichment.summary: Lockwood grumbles about his lengthy illness and confinement at Thrushcross Grange during the bleak northern winter.

context: This is the opening passage of the chapter, spoken by Mr. Lockwood, the narrator and tenant at Thrushcross Grange. He is complaining about his illness and isolation during his first weeks at the property, expressing frustration with the harsh Yorkshire weather, poor medical care from the country surgeon Kenneth, and the lack of social company. This sets the scene for his request to Mrs. Dean to continue her story about Heathcliff's past.

Mr. Heathcliff has just honoured me with a call. About seven days ago he sent
me a brace of grouse—the last of the season. Scoundrel! He is not
altogether guiltless in this illness of mine; and that I had a great mind to
tell him. But, alas! how could I offend a man who was charitable enough to sit
at my bedside a good hour, and talk on some other subject than pills and
draughts, blisters and leeches? This is quite an easy interval. I am too weak
to read; yet I feel as if I could enjoy something interesting. Why not have up
Mrs. Dean to finish her tale? I can recollect its chief incidents, as far as
she had gone. Yes: I remember her hero had run off, and never been heard of for
three years; and the heroine was married. I’ll ring: she’ll be
delighted to find me capable of talking cheerfully. Mrs. Dean came.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lockwood's characterization develops; his decision to have Nelly continue her tale propels the narrative forward and reveals his impatience to hear about Heathcliff.
enrichment.best_quote: Why not have up Mrs. Dean to finish her tale?
enrichment.summary: Lockwood receives a call from Heathcliff, reflects on his generosity despite suspecting his involvement in the illness, and requests Nelly resume her narrative about Heathcliff's mysterious absence and Catherine's marriage.

“With all my heart! Don’t interrupt me. Come and take your seat
here. Keep your fingers from that bitter phalanx of vials. Draw your knitting
out of your pocket—that will do—now continue the history of Mr.
Heathcliff, from where you left off, to the present day. Did he finish his
education on the Continent, and come back a gentleman? or did he get a
sizar’s place at college, or escape to America, and earn honours by
drawing blood from his foster-country? or make a fortune more promptly on the
English highways?”

couldn’t give my word for any. I stated before that I didn’t know
how he gained his money; neither am I aware of the means he took to raise his
mind from the savage ignorance into which it was sunk: but, with your leave,
I’ll proceed in my own fashion, if you think it will amuse and not weary

text:
I got Miss Catherine and myself to Thrushcross Grange; and, to my agreeable
disappointment, she behaved infinitely better than I dared to expect. She
seemed almost over-fond of Mr. Linton; and even to his sister she showed plenty
of affection. They were both very attentive to her comfort, certainly. It was
not the thorn bending to the honeysuckles, but the honeysuckles embracing the
thorn. There were no mutual concessions: one stood erect, and the others
yielded: and who  can  be ill-natured and bad-tempered when they encounter
neither opposition nor indifference? I observed that Mr. Edgar had a
deep-rooted fear of ruffling her humour. He concealed it from her; but if ever
he heard me answer sharply, or saw any other servant grow cloudy at some
imperious order of hers, he would show his trouble by a frown of displeasure
that never darkened on his own account. He many a time spoke sternly to me
about my pertness; and averred that the stab of a knife could not inflict a
worse pang than he suffered at seeing his lady vexed. Not to grieve a kind
master, I learned to be less touchy; and, for the space of half a year, the
gunpowder lay as harmless as sand, because no fire came near to explode it.
Catherine had seasons of gloom and silence now and then: they were respected
with sympathising silence by her husband, who ascribed them to an alteration in
her constitution, produced by her perilous illness; as she was never subject to
depression of spirits before. The return of sunshine was welcomed by answering
sunshine from him. I believe I may assert that they were really in possession
of deep and growing happiness.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended, lyrical passage depicting Catherine Linton and Edgar's early married happiness at Thrushcross Grange; reveals complex character dynamics and foreshadows their deterioration.
enrichment.best_quote: It was not the thorn bending to the honeysuckles, but the honeysuckles embracing the thorn.
enrichment.summary: Nelly describes Catherine's initial contentment at Thrushcross Grange after marriage, noting her affection for Edgar Linton and his anxious devotion; she enjoyed six months of genuine happiness before her temperament showed signs of melancholy.

context: This passage describes Nelly Dean's account of Catherine's early married life at Thrushcross Grange with Edgar Linton. It depicts Catherine's surprisingly good behavior toward the Linton family, Edgar's devoted and indulgent treatment of her, and the apparent happiness of their marriage during the first six months, before Heathcliff's unexpected return disrupts their domestic peace.

text:
It ended. Well, we  must  be for ourselves in the long run; the mild and
generous are only more justly selfish than the domineering; and it ended when
circumstances caused each to feel that the one’s interest was not the
chief consideration in the other’s thoughts. On a mellow evening in
September, I was coming from the garden with a heavy basket of apples which I
had been gathering. It had got dusk, and the moon looked over the high wall of
the court, causing undefined shadows to lurk in the corners of the numerous
projecting portions of the building. I set my burden on the house-steps by the
kitchen-door, and lingered to rest, and drew in a few more breaths of the soft,
sweet air; my eyes were on the moon, and my back to the entrance, when I heard
a voice behind me say,—“Nelly, is that you?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Pivotal shift marked by atmospheric Gothic diction; Nelly's discovery of Heathcliff's mysterious return creates dramatic suspense and begins the climactic entanglement.
enrichment.best_quote: Nelly, is that you?
enrichment.summary: Nelly finds herself approached by an unknown voice in the dusk beside Thrushcross Grange; the mysterious visitor reveals himself, initiating Heathcliff's fateful reappearance after three years' absence.

context: This passage marks the turning point in Catherine and Edgar Linton's marriage at Thrushcross Grange. After a period of genuine happiness together, their contentment ends when mutual self-interest replaces mutual consideration. The narrator, Nelly Dean, is about to encounter Heathcliff's mysterious return to the neighborhood after a three-year absence, which will set in motion the dramatic events that follow.

text:
It was a deep voice, and foreign in tone; yet there was something in the manner
of pronouncing my name which made it sound familiar. I turned about to discover
who spoke, fearfully; for the doors were shut, and I had seen nobody on
approaching the steps. Something stirred in the porch; and, moving nearer, I
distinguished a tall man dressed in dark clothes, with dark face and hair. He
leant against the side, and held his fingers on the latch as if intending to
open for himself. “Who can it be?” I thought. “Mr. Earnshaw?
Oh, no! The voice has no resemblance to his.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Heightened mystery and recognition scene; Nelly's emotional response and initial uncertainty build suspense before the revelation.
enrichment.best_quote: Who can it be?
enrichment.summary: Nelly struggles to identify the stranger in the darkness, noting his foreign accent and physical bearing before recognizing his distinctive eyes.

context: Nelly Dean encounters Heathcliff's mysterious return to Thrushcross Grange after a three-year absence. “I have waited here an hour,” he resumed, while I continued
staring; “and the whole of that time all round has been as still as
death. I dared not enter. You do not know me? Look, I’m not a
stranger!”

visitor, and I raised my hands in amazement. “What! you come back? Is it

“Yes, Heathcliff,” he replied, glancing from me up to the windows,
which reflected a score of glittering moons, but showed no lights from within.
“Are they at home? where is she? Nelly, you are not glad! you
needn’t be so disturbed. Is she here? Speak! I want to have one word with
her—your mistress. Go, and say some person from Gimmerton desires to see
her.”

Mrs. Linton were, I could not persuade myself to proceed. At length I resolved

They sat together in a window whose lattice lay back against the wall, and
displayed, beyond the garden trees, and the wild green park, the valley of
Gimmerton, with a long line of mist winding nearly to its top (for very soon
after you pass the chapel, as you may have noticed, the sough that runs from
the marshes joins a beck which follows the bend of the glen). Wuthering Heights
rose above this silvery vapour; but our old house was invisible; it rather dips
down on the other side. Both the room and its occupants, and the scene they
gazed on, looked wondrously peaceful. I shrank reluctantly from performing my
errand; and was actually going away leaving it unsaid, after having put my
question about the candles, when a sense of my folly compelled me to return,
and mutter, “A person from Gimmerton wishes to see you
ma’am.”

Mr. Linton walked to a window on the other side of the room that overlooked the
court. He unfastened it, and leant out. I suppose they were below, for he
exclaimed quickly: “Don’t stand there, love! Bring the person in,
if it be anyone particular.” Ere long, I heard the click of the latch,
and Catherine flew upstairs, breathless and wild; too excited to show gladness:
indeed, by her face, you would rather have surmised an awful calamity.

I descended, and found Heathcliff waiting under the porch, evidently
anticipating an invitation to enter. He followed my guidance without waste of
words, and I ushered him into the presence of the master and mistress, whose
flushed cheeks betrayed signs of warm talking. But the lady’s glowed with
another feeling when her friend appeared at the door: she sprang forward, took
both his hands, and led him to Linton; and then she seized Linton’s
reluctant fingers and crushed them into his. Now, fully revealed by the fire
and candlelight, I was amazed, more than ever, to behold the transformation of
Heathcliff. He had grown a tall, athletic, well-formed man; beside whom my
master seemed quite slender and youth-like. His upright carriage suggested the
idea of his having been in the army. His countenance was much older in
expression and decision of feature than Mr. Linton’s; it looked
intelligent, and retained no marks of former degradation. A half-civilised
ferocity lurked yet in the depressed brows and eyes full of black fire, but it
was subdued; and his manner was even dignified: quite divested of roughness,
though too stern for grace. My master’s surprise equalled or exceeded
mine: he remained for a minute at a loss how to address the ploughboy, as he
had called him. Heathcliff dropped his slight hand, and stood looking at him
coolly till he chose to speak.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The transformative reunion scene; Heathcliff's physical and social metamorphosis is vividly described, creating dramatic irony and revealing the complexity beneath his altered exterior.
enrichment.best_quote: Now, fully revealed by the fire and candlelight, I was amazed, more than ever, to behold the transformation of Heathcliff. He had grown a tall, athletic, well-formed man; beside whom my master seemed quite slender and youth-like.
enrichment.summary: Nelly escorts Heathcliff into the parlour where Catherine eagerly greets him and introduces him to Edgar; Nelly observes his remarkable physical transformation—he is now a striking, dignified man whose intelligence and bearing surpass Edgar's, though a suppressed ferocity still lurks beneath his composed exterior.

heard of your marriage, Cathy, not long since; and, while waiting in the yard
below, I meditated this plan—just to have one glimpse of your face, a
stare of surprise, perhaps, and pretended pleasure; afterwards settle my score
with Hindley; and then prevent the law by doing execution on myself. Your
welcome has put these ideas out of my mind; but beware of meeting me with
another aspect next time! Nay, you’ll not drive me off again. You were
really sorry for me, were you? Well, there was cause. I’ve fought through
a bitter life since I last heard your voice; and you must forgive me, for I
struggled only for you!”

the walls. I was endeavouring to gather resolution for entering and taking
possession, when my fool of a guide announced,—“This here is

And so he went on scolding to his den beneath, taking the candle with him; and
I remained in the dark. The period of reflection succeeding this silly action
compelled me to admit the necessity of smothering my pride and choking my
wrath, and bestirring myself to remove its effects. An unexpected aid presently
appeared in the shape of Throttler, whom I now recognised as a son of our old
Skulker: it had spent its whelphood at the Grange, and was given by my father
to Mr. Hindley. I fancy it knew me: it pushed its nose against mine by way of
salute, and then hastened to devour the porridge; while I groped from step to
step, collecting the shattered earthenware, and drying the spatters of milk
from the banister with my pocket-handkerchief. Our labours were scarcely over
when I heard Earnshaw’s tread in the passage; my assistant tucked in his
tail, and pressed to the wall; I stole into the nearest doorway. The
dog’s endeavour to avoid him was unsuccessful; as I guessed by a scutter
downstairs, and a prolonged, piteous yelping. I had better luck: he passed on,
entered his chamber, and shut the door. Directly after Joseph came up with
Hareton, to put him to bed. I had found shelter in Hareton’s room, and
the old man, on seeing me, said,—“They’s rahm for boath ye
un’ yer pride, now, I sud think i’ the hahse. It’s empty; ye
may hev’ it all to yerseln, un’ Him as allas maks a third, i’
sich ill company!”

demanded, in his loving manner, what I was doing there? I told him the cause of
my staying up so late—that he had the key of our room in his pocket. The
adjective  our  gave mortal offence. He swore it was not, nor ever should
be, mine; and he’d—but I’ll not repeat his language, nor
describe his habitual conduct: he is ingenious and unresting in seeking to gain
my abhorrence! I sometimes wonder at him with an intensity that deadens my
fear: yet, I assure you, a tiger or a venomous serpent could not rouse terror
in me equal to that which he wakens. He told me of Catherine’s illness,
and accused my brother of causing it; promising that I should be Edgar’s
proxy in suffering, till he could get hold of him.
